brief.audience: curious kids and adults who use the internet daily but have never wondered what happens when they hit send
brief.learningGoal: Explain that a video is chopped into numbered, separately addressed packets forwarded hop by hop by routers with no master map, which is why the internet keeps working when a link breaks.
brief.hook: You hit send, and your video feels like one unbroken stream. It isn't.

shots.purpose: hook-continuous-stream-myth: Challenge the one-stream assumption and pose the question with a payoff.
shots.narration: You hit send on a video. It feels like one unbroken stream across the world. It isn't. So how does it arrive intact, even if a cable breaks?
shots.headline: Not one stream

shots.purpose: chop-into-packets: Teach slicing, addressing and numbering before they are needed.
shots.narration: Your device slices the video into thousands of small packets. Each gets its own from and to address, and a sequence number. Each packet is independent.
shots.headline: Thousands of packets

shots.purpose: hop-by-hop-no-map: Explain hop-by-hop forwarding with the postcard image.
shots.narration: Think of postcards and sorting offices. Each router reads the address, checks its short list, and hands the packet to the next one. None of them knows the whole route.
shots.headline: Sorting offices

shots.lyric: Chopped up. Addressed. Passed hand to hand.

shots.purpose: resolution-reassembly-resilience: Resolve: rerouting around breaks and reordering on arrival.
shots.narration: If a link breaks, routers update their lists and packets can detour. At the end, the numbers put them back in order. No single path or map to break.
shots.headline: No single path to break
